entries.label: verb phrase
entries.meaning: To consider a particular fact or factor when you judge a situation or make a decision.
entries.usage: Very common in speech and writing, from casual advice to official reports. A short object usually goes in the middle (*take the weather into account*); a long one goes at the end (*take into account the fact that …*). The passive *be taken into account* is frequent in formal writing, and *take into consideration* is a slightly more formal variant.
entries.pattern: take + noun + into account / take into account + long noun phrase
examples: When you compare the two job offers, **take** the commute **into account**, not just the salary.
The price looks low, but once you **take** shipping and taxes **into account**, it's not much of a bargain.
The judge said she had **taken into account** the defendant's age and clean record.

drill.sentence: Our estimate for the kitchen remodel didn't {{take into account}} the cost of moving the gas line.
drill.hint: consider as part of the calculation (three words with *into*; not *factor in*)

mistake.wrong: We didn't take in account the time difference.
mistake.right: We didn't take into account the time difference.
mistake.why: The fixed preposition is *into*: *take something into account*.

entries.related: *factor in* — informal, often about costs or time; *take into consideration* — more formal; *allow for* — plan for something that may happen.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: One of the most important causes or influences that decide how something turns out.
entries.usage: Common in news, business, sports commentary and careful conversation. Typical patterns are *a key factor in* + noun or *-ing* and *be a key factor*; *the key factor* means the single most important one. *A major factor* and *an important factor* are close alternatives.
entries.pattern: a key factor in + noun / -ing
examples: Location was **a key factor** in our decision to rent the smaller apartment.
Doctors say poor sleep can be **a key factor** in high blood pressure.
Their goalkeeper's injury was **a key factor** in the team's early exit from the tournament.

drill.sentence: Experts say the cold, wet spring was {{a key factor}} in this year's poor apple harvest.
drill.hint: one of the main causes (a one-syllable adjective; not *big* or *main*)

entries.related: *a major factor* — very similar; *a contributing factor* — one of several causes, often of something bad; *the deciding factor* — the one that finally settles a choice.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: Before a particular time or event, so that something is ready or arranged early.
entries.usage: Very common in speech, emails and instructions, usually after the verb: *book, pay, plan* or *prepare in advance*. To say how early, put the time first (*two weeks in advance*); *well in advance of* + noun is more formal. The email closing *Thanks in advance* is common, though some readers find it a little pushy.
entries.pattern: verb + in advance; two days / a week in advance; in advance of + noun
examples: Tickets for the museum sell out fast, so it's best to book them online **in advance**.
If you need a vegetarian meal on the flight, you usually have to request it at least a day **in advance**.
The city announced the road closures well **in advance** of the marathon.

drill.sentence: Let me know {{in advance}} if you can't make it, so I can give your seat to someone else.
drill.hint: before the day itself (a prepositional phrase; not *ahead of time* or *beforehand*)

mistake.wrong: Thanks in advanced for your help.
mistake.right: Thanks in advance for your help.
mistake.why: The phrase uses the noun *advance*; *advanced* is an adjective meaning "at a high level".

entries.related: *ahead of time* — same meaning, more casual; *beforehand* — before an event already mentioned; *early* — before the usual or expected time.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To help more people know about and understand an issue, usually a health, social or safety problem.
entries.usage: Typical of charities, campaigns, health services and news reports. The patterns are *raise awareness of / about / for* + issue and *raise awareness that* + clause; *raise public awareness* is a frequent variant. It is sometimes used critically, when a campaign creates attention but no real change.
entries.pattern: raise (public) awareness of / about / for + issue
examples: The 5K run is meant to **raise awareness** of mental health problems among college students.
My sister wears a pink ribbon every October to **raise awareness** about breast cancer.
The library is running free workshops to **raise awareness** of online scams that target older adults.

drill.sentence: Every May, the clinic hands out free sunscreen to {{raise awareness}} about skin cancer.
drill.hint: help more people know and understand (the verb is not *spread* or *increase*)

mistake.wrong: The campaign wants to rise awareness of dementia.
mistake.right: The campaign wants to raise awareness of dementia.
mistake.why: *Raise* takes an object (you raise something); *rise* has no object (prices rise).

entries.related: *draw attention to* — make people notice something; *spread the word* — informal, tell many people; *campaign for* — work actively for a change.

entries.label: verb phrase
entries.meaning: To feel hurt or offended by a remark or event as if it were aimed at you, when it was not.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation, especially as reassurance: *Don't take it personally.* The object comes between *take* and *personally*, usually *it*, *this* or *that*. It can also describe someone who reacts too strongly to criticism: *He takes every bad review personally.*
entries.pattern: take it / something personally; don't take it personally
examples: She didn't answer your text because she was busy, so don't **take it personally**.
The coach yells at everyone during practice, and the players have learned not to **take it personally**.
Our new neighbor **took it personally** when we put up a fence, but we just wanted to keep the dog in.

drill.sentence: My cat ignores everyone who visits, so please don't {{take it personally}} if she hides from you.
drill.hint: feel hurt, as if it were about you (verb + *it* + adverb; not *be offended*)

entries.related: *take something to heart* — be deeply affected by criticism or advice; *take offense (at)* — feel insulted; *it's nothing personal* — the speaker's reassurance.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To finish a piece of work by the time it is due.
entries.usage: Very common at work, in school and in journalism. The usual verb is *meet*; the opposite is *miss a deadline*, and a deadline can be *tight*, *extended* or *pushed back*. *Make the deadline* is also common in casual speech.
entries.pattern: meet / miss a (tight) deadline
examples: The builders worked through the night to **meet the deadline** for the new stadium.
If you can't **meet the deadline**, tell your editor now, not the night before.
Students who don't **meet the deadline** for financial aid can lose thousands of dollars.

drill.sentence: The contractor promised to finish the bathroom by Friday, but I doubt he'll {{meet the deadline}}.
drill.hint: finish on time (the verb is not *make*)

mistake.wrong: We managed to keep the deadline.
mistake.right: We managed to meet the deadline.
mistake.why: German *eine Frist einhalten* leads learners to *keep*; in English you *meet* a deadline, and *keep* goes with *a promise* or *an appointment*.

entries.related: *miss a deadline* — the opposite; *beat the deadline* — finish before it; *push back a deadline* — move it later.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A wrong belief or idea that many people share.
entries.usage: Common in journalism, teaching, health advice and conversation, usually just before the speaker corrects it: *It's a common misconception that …* Other frequent patterns are *a common misconception about* + noun and *one of the most common misconceptions*. *A popular misconception* is a close variant.
entries.pattern: it's a common misconception that … / a common misconception about + noun
examples: It's **a common misconception** that goldfish only remember things for a few seconds.
**A common misconception** about freelancers is that they can take a day off whenever they want.
Many patients still think antibiotics cure colds, which is **a common misconception**.

drill.sentence: Wearing a hat helps, but the idea that you lose most of your body heat through your head is {{a common misconception}}.
drill.hint: a false belief that many people share (not *myth*; the adjective is not *popular* or *widespread*)

entries.related: *a myth* — more casual, a false story or belief; *a popular belief* — neutral, not necessarily wrong; *a misunderstanding* — a failure to understand a specific situation.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: Responsible for and in control of a person, group, task or place.
entries.usage: Very common at work and in everyday life: *be in charge of* + noun or *-ing*, and *put someone in charge of* something. *The person in charge* means the boss or manager. Don't confuse it with *free of charge*, which means costing nothing.
entries.pattern: be in charge of + noun / -ing; put someone in charge of + noun
examples: Who's **in charge of** the music at the wedding reception?
My older brother was **in charge of** cooking the turkey this Thanksgiving, and it came out a little dry.
After the holiday travel chaos, the airline put a new manager **in charge of** customer complaints.

drill.sentence: While the principal is away, Ms. Rivera is {{in charge of}} the school.
drill.hint: the person who controls and manages (not *responsible for* or *running*)

mistake.wrong: Who is in charge for the budget?
mistake.right: Who is in charge of the budget?
mistake.why: The fixed preposition is *of*; *for* belongs to *responsible for*.

entries.related: *responsible for* — similar, but stresses duty or blame more than control; *run* — manage a business or event; *oversee* — more formal, watch over other people's work.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To agree on something after a discussion or negotiation, often after some difficulty.
entries.usage: Typical of news, business and law, and also used about families and couples. Patterns are *reach an agreement with* someone, *on / over* something, or *to* + verb. *Come to an agreement* is a slightly more casual equivalent; *strike a deal* sounds more active and journalistic.
entries.pattern: reach an agreement (with someone) on / over + noun; reach an agreement to + verb
examples: After three days of talks, the union and the hospital finally **reached an agreement** on pay.
My ex and I **reached an agreement** about who gets the kids for the holidays.
The team couldn't **reach an agreement** with its star pitcher on a new contract, so he's signing elsewhere.

drill.sentence: The landlord and the tenants {{reached an agreement}}: rent goes up three percent, and he'll fix the elevator.
drill.hint: settled the terms after talks (the verb is not *came to*)

entries.related: *come to an agreement* — same, slightly more casual; *strike a deal* — more active, common in news; *agree to disagree* — accept that you won't agree.

entries.label: adverb + verb
entries.meaning: To think carefully about something as a real possibility, not just as a passing idea.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, news and advice, often about big personal decisions: *I'm seriously considering moving.* It takes a noun or an *-ing* form, never *to* + verb. It also appears in the passive: *The idea is being seriously considered.*
entries.pattern: seriously consider + noun / -ing
examples: With three kids in a two-bedroom apartment, we're **seriously considering** a bigger place.
She's **seriously considering** going back to school to become a nurse.
The town council says it will **seriously consider** a ban on gas-powered leaf blowers.

drill.sentence: My knees hurt after every run, so I'm {{seriously considering}} switching to swimming.
drill.hint: treating as a real option (adverb + verb; not *thinking about*)

mistake.wrong: I'm seriously considering to quit my job.
mistake.right: I'm seriously considering quitting my job.
mistake.why: *Consider* is followed by a noun or an *-ing* form, not by *to* + verb.

entries.related: *think about* — more casual and less committed; *weigh* — compare the good and bad sides; *toy with the idea of* — consider without being serious.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To believe that something is true without having proof of it.
entries.usage: Common in speech and writing, and often slightly critical: *You're making a lot of assumptions.* Patterns are *make assumptions about* + noun and *make the assumption that* + clause. In more formal writing, people also *work on the assumption that* …
entries.pattern: make an assumption about + noun; make the assumption that + clause
examples: Don't **make assumptions** about people based on how they dress.
You're **making a big assumption** if you think the bus will actually show up on time.
The city's budget **makes the assumption** that tax revenue will grow by five percent next year.

drill.sentence: He {{made the assumption}} that the store would be open on Sunday and drove forty minutes for nothing.
drill.hint: believed it without checking (verb + noun)

entries.related: *assume* — the one-word verb; *jump to conclusions* — decide too quickly, critical; *take something for granted* — assume without thinking about it.

entries.label: noun phrase
entries.meaning: More and more people or things; a number that keeps increasing.
entries.usage: Common in news, reports and formal speech to describe a trend. It takes a plural noun, and the verb is plural too: *A growing number of people are …*. *An increasing number of* is a close, slightly more formal variant.
entries.pattern: a growing number of + plural noun + plural verb
examples: **A growing number of** Americans are choosing to rent rather than buy a home.
In our area, **a growing number of** restaurants now add a service fee to the bill.
Pediatricians are seeing **a growing number of** teenagers with injuries from playing one sport all year.

drill.sentence: {{A growing number of}} parents are keeping their kids off social media until high school.
drill.hint: more and more (the adjective is not *increasing*)

mistake.wrong: A growing number of people is working from home.
mistake.right: A growing number of people are working from home.
mistake.why: After *a number of* + plural noun, the verb is plural, because the people are the real subject.

entries.related: *an increasing number of* — same, slightly more formal; *more and more* — plainer, spoken; *the number of* — takes a singular verb: *The number of cases is rising.*

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: In a situation where something bad, such as harm, loss or failure, may happen.
entries.usage: Common in health, social services, news and finance. Patterns are *be at risk of* + noun or *-ing* (*at risk of losing their homes*) and *put someone or something at risk*. Before a noun it is hyphenated: *at-risk youth*, *at-risk students*.
entries.pattern: be at risk of + noun / -ing; put + noun + at risk
examples: People who sit all day are more **at risk** of back problems.
Hundreds of homes along the river are **at risk** if the levee breaks.
Texting while driving puts everyone on the road **at risk**.

drill.sentence: Older people who live alone are especially {{at risk}} during heat waves.
drill.hint: likely to be harmed (two words; not *in danger*)

mistake.wrong: Many species are in risk of extinction.
mistake.right: Many species are at risk of extinction.
mistake.why: The preposition is *at*: *at risk*, although the similar phrase is *in danger*.

entries.related: *in danger* — similar, a bit more dramatic; *at stake* — what could be lost, not who could be harmed; *vulnerable* — easily hurt.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To decide that something is true after thinking about the facts or evidence.
entries.usage: Common in academic writing, journalism and careful conversation, often with *from*: *draw conclusions from the results*. Typical warnings are *It's too early to draw any conclusions* and *Don't draw conclusions too quickly*. *Reach* and *come to a conclusion* are also correct, while *jump to conclusions* means to decide too fast.
entries.pattern: draw a conclusion (from + evidence); draw the conclusion that + clause; draw your own conclusions
examples: One bad game isn't enough to **draw any conclusions** about the new quarterback.
From the empty fridge and the pile of dishes, I **drew the conclusion** that my roommate was back.
The study was too small to **draw firm conclusions** about the drug's long-term effects.

drill.sentence: I'm not going to tell you what I think of her new boyfriend; you can {{draw your own conclusions}}.
drill.hint: decide for yourself what it means (the verb is not *reach* or *come to*)

mistake.wrong: What conclusion can we make from these numbers?
mistake.right: What conclusion can we draw from these numbers?
mistake.why: *Conclusion* goes with *draw*, *reach* or *come to*; *make a conclusion* sounds wrong to most native speakers.

entries.related: *come to / reach a conclusion* — decide after thinking; *jump to conclusions* — decide too fast, critical; *infer* — the formal one-word verb.

entries.label: verb + adverb
entries.meaning: To work from home or another place instead of at the employer's office, usually connected online.
entries.usage: Very common since the pandemic, in job ads, HR language and conversation. Related forms are *remote work*, *a remote job* and *work from home* (*WFH* in casual writing). *Fully remote* means never in the office; *hybrid* means part of the week in the office.
entries.pattern: work remotely (from + place); a remote job; fully remote / hybrid
examples: Since I started **working remotely**, I've saved two hours a day on commuting.
The job ad says you can **work remotely**, but they want you in the office once a month.
My cousin **works remotely** from a small town in Vermont for a company based in Seattle.

drill.sentence: Her company lets employees {{work remotely}} two days a week, so she only goes into the office on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays.
drill.hint: do their jobs away from the office (verb + adverb; not *from home*)

mistake.wrong: I'm working in home office today.
mistake.right: I'm working from home today.
mistake.why: German *Homeoffice* means working from home, but in English a *home office* is a room in your home; the activity is *working from home* or *working remotely*.

entries.related: *work from home* — the everyday spoken phrase; *telecommute* — older and a bit dated; *hybrid* — partly remote, partly in the office.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To say openly or officially that you are worried about something, so that others pay attention to it.
entries.usage: Common in meetings, news, official reports and complaints. Patterns are *raise concerns about / over* + noun and *raise concerns that* + clause; the subject can be a person or a fact (*The results raise concerns*). It sounds more formal than *say you're worried*.
entries.pattern: raise concerns about / over + noun; raise concerns that + clause
examples: Several parents **raised concerns** about the lack of crossing guards near the school.
The nurse **raised concerns** with her supervisor that the night shift was dangerously understaffed.
The sudden jump in prices has **raised concerns** that some families won't be able to heat their homes this winter.

drill.sentence: At my dog's checkup, the vet {{raised concerns}} about his weight and suggested smaller meals.
drill.hint: said openly that she was worried (the verb is not *voiced* or *expressed*)

entries.related: *voice concerns* — very similar, a bit more formal; *express concern* — often singular, polite; *raise the alarm* — warn strongly about a danger.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: Stressed because of demands, expectations or a lack of time, or pushed by others to do something.
entries.usage: Very common in speech and writing about work, sports, school and family. Patterns are *be / feel / work under pressure*, *under pressure to* + verb and *under pressure from* + person or group. *Under a lot of pressure* is frequent, and *work well under pressure* is a job-ad cliché.
entries.pattern: be / feel / work under pressure (to + verb / from + someone)
examples: I'm **under a lot of pressure** at work right now, so I can't take a vacation.
Air traffic controllers have to make quick decisions **under pressure** all day long.
The mayor is **under pressure** from residents to fix the potholes before winter.

drill.sentence: Many teenagers feel {{under pressure}} to look perfect on social media.
drill.hint: pushed by other people's expectations (preposition + noun)

entries.related: *stressed out* — informal, the feeling; *under strain* — under heavy difficulty, often financial or physical; *pressure someone into* + *-ing* — force someone to do something.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To have a clear, noticeable effect on something or someone.
entries.usage: Common in speech and writing, from business reports to everyday talk. Adjectives often go before *impact*: *a big, huge, positive, negative, lasting* or *real impact*. The preposition is *on*; *impact* is also used as a verb (*impact sales*), but some editors prefer *affect*.
entries.pattern: have a (big / positive / lasting) impact on + noun
examples: Moving to a new country **had a huge impact on** my kids, but they adjusted quickly.
Small changes, like taking the stairs, can **have a real impact on** your health.
The long drought **had a devastating impact on** this year's apple harvest.

drill.sentence: My high school chemistry teacher {{had an impact on}} my decision to become a pharmacist.
drill.hint: clearly affected (verb + noun + preposition; the noun is not *influence* or *effect*)

entries.related: *have an effect on* — plainer and more neutral; *affect* — the one-word verb; *make a difference* — have a positive effect.

entries.label: adverb + verb
entries.meaning: To disagree completely and firmly with an opinion, idea or decision.
entries.usage: Common in debates, meetings, opinion pieces and surveys (*strongly agree … strongly disagree*). The patterns are *strongly disagree with* + person or idea and *strongly disagree that* + clause. Face to face it can sound blunt; *I'm not sure I agree* or *I see it differently* are softer.
entries.pattern: strongly disagree with + someone / something; strongly disagree that + clause
examples: I **strongly disagree** with the idea that kids should have homework every night.
Many longtime fans **strongly disagreed** with the team's decision to trade its best player.
In the survey, forty percent of employees **strongly disagreed** that their workload was manageable.

drill.sentence: You think pineapple doesn't belong on pizza? I {{strongly disagree}}; it's the best topping there is.
drill.hint: firmly don't share that view (the adverb is not *completely* or *totally*)

mistake.wrong: I'm strongly disagree with this plan.
mistake.right: I strongly disagree with this plan.
mistake.why: *Disagree* is a full verb, so it takes no *am*; the error often comes from *be* + *agree* phrases such as Spanish *estar de acuerdo*.

entries.related: *beg to differ* — polite, a little formal or humorous; *take issue with* — disagree with one specific point; *object to* — formally oppose.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: Almost all of the people or things in a group.
entries.usage: Common in speech, news and academic writing, usually as *the vast majority of* + plural noun with a plural verb: *The vast majority of residents support the plan.* It can also stand alone: *The vast majority agree.* *The overwhelming majority* is a close, slightly stronger variant.
entries.pattern: the vast majority of + plural noun (+ plural verb)
examples: **The vast majority of** our customers pay by card, so we rarely see cash anymore.
The festival was a success: **the vast majority** of visitors said they would come back next year.
On our street, **the vast majority of** the houses were built in the 1950s.

drill.sentence: Only a handful of people complained; {{the vast majority}} of guests loved the new menu.
drill.hint: almost all (the adjective is not *overwhelming* or *great*)

entries.related: *the overwhelming majority* — same, slightly stronger; *most* — plainer; *a slim majority* — just over half.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To accept that something is your duty, or that a mistake or problem is your fault.
entries.usage: Common at work, in parenting, news and apologies; it sounds mature and honest. The pattern is *take responsibility for* + noun or *-ing*, often with *full*: *I take full responsibility.* *Accept responsibility* is more formal.
entries.pattern: take (full) responsibility for + noun / -ing
examples: The restaurant manager **took full responsibility** for the mix-up and didn't charge us for dinner.
At sixteen, my son finally started **taking responsibility for** his own laundry.
Good leaders **take responsibility** when things go wrong instead of blaming their team.

drill.sentence: He broke the window with his baseball, and to his credit, he {{took responsibility}} and offered to pay for it.
drill.hint: admitted it was his fault (the noun is not *blame*)

mistake.wrong: You need to take responsibility of your actions.
mistake.right: You need to take responsibility for your actions.
mistake.why: After *take responsibility*, the thing you are responsible for follows *for*.

entries.related: *own up to* — informal, admit a mistake; *take the blame* — accept fault, sometimes for others; *be accountable* — be required to explain your actions.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: Making progress as planned, so that a goal is likely to be reached on time.
entries.usage: Very common at work and in sports, finance and personal goals. Patterns are *be on track to* + verb, *be on track for* + noun, *stay on track* and *get back on track*. The opposite is *off track*; *on the right track* means that your approach is correct.
entries.pattern: be on track to + verb / for + noun; stay on track; get back on track
examples: After a slow start, the new library is back **on track** to open in the spring.
I'm saving three hundred dollars a month, so I'm **on track** for a trip to Japan next summer.
With five games left, the team is **on track** to make the playoffs for the first time in a decade.

drill.sentence: I ate a lot of cookies over the holidays, but I'm getting back {{on track}} with my diet now.
drill.hint: following the plan again (preposition + noun)

entries.related: *on schedule* — exactly at the planned time; *on the right track* — using a good approach; *off track* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To do something practical to deal with a problem, rather than only talk about it.
entries.usage: Common in news, business and campaigns, often with a sense of urgency: *It's time to take action.* Adjectives are frequent: *immediate, urgent, legal* or *decisive action*. Typical patterns are *take action to* + verb and *take action against* someone.
entries.pattern: take (immediate / legal) action (to + verb / against + someone)
examples: If the landlord doesn't fix the heat by Friday, we'll **take legal action**.
The school **took action** right away after parents reported bullying on the bus.
Talking about saving money is easy; **taking action** is the hard part.

drill.sentence: We've complained about the broken streetlight for months, and the city still hasn't {{taken action}}.
drill.hint: dealt with it in practice (verb + noun)

mistake.wrong: The city must take an action now.
mistake.right: The city must take action now.
mistake.why: In this phrase *action* is uncountable, so there is no *an*.

entries.related: *take steps* — do specific things toward a goal; *act* — the one-word verb; *crack down on* — take strong action against wrongdoing.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: An angry, emotional discussion in which people disagree strongly.
entries.usage: Common in news and conversation about sports, local issues, family and work. Typical patterns are *a heated debate about / over* + topic, *spark a heated debate* and *get into a heated debate*. *Heated* also goes with *argument*, *discussion* and *exchange*.
entries.pattern: a heated debate about / over + topic; spark / get into a heated debate
examples: My wife and I got into **a heated debate** about whether a hot dog counts as a sandwich.
The plan to cut down the old oak trees led to **a heated debate** at the town meeting.
There's **a heated debate** online over whether the new phone is worth the price.

drill.sentence: The referee's call in the final minute sparked {{a heated debate}} among fans that's still going on.
drill.hint: an angry exchange of views (the adjective is not *fierce*; the noun is not *argument* or *discussion*)

entries.related: *a lively debate* — energetic but friendly; *a heated argument* — more personal, often between two people; *a shouting match* — informal, very angry.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To do specific, practical things in order to reach a result or deal with a problem.
entries.usage: Common in official statements, news, business and health advice. The pattern is *take steps to* + verb, often with *concrete, practical, immediate* or *important*. It sounds more planned and careful than *take action*.
entries.pattern: take (concrete / practical) steps to + verb
examples: The hotel has **taken steps to** reduce plastic waste, like replacing tiny shampoo bottles with refillable dispensers.
If you think someone has stolen your identity, **take steps to** protect your credit right away.
The school district is **taking steps to** make its buses safer, including adding seat belts.

drill.sentence: After two workers got sick in the July heat, the farm {{took steps to}} protect its crews, such as starting work at dawn.
drill.hint: did specific things in order to (the noun is not *measures* or *action*)

entries.related: *take measures* — more formal, often official; *take action* — act in general; *take the first step* — begin a process.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: Stopped or delayed for a period of time, with the plan to continue later.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, at work and in the news; the usual patterns are *put something on hold* and *be on hold*. Typical objects are plans, projects, careers and hiring. On the phone, *on hold* means waiting to be connected, which is a separate sense.
entries.pattern: put + noun + on hold; be on hold
examples: We've put our wedding plans **on hold** until we both find jobs in the same city.
Work on the new bridge is **on hold** because of a dispute over costs.
She put her career **on hold** for five years to raise her kids.

drill.sentence: The band's world tour is {{on hold}} while the drummer recovers from a hand injury.
drill.hint: paused, to continue later (not *on ice* or *on hiatus*)

entries.related: *on ice* — informal, paused for a long time; *put off* — postpone to a later date; *on the back burner* — given low priority.

entries.label: adverb + adjective
entries.meaning: Very worried about something serious.
entries.usage: Typical of official statements, news and serious conversation; it sounds formal and grave. Patterns are *deeply concerned about / by* + noun and *deeply concerned that* + clause. In casual speech people more often say *really worried*.
entries.pattern: be deeply concerned about / by + noun; deeply concerned that + clause
examples: Teachers are **deeply concerned** about the number of students who regularly skip class.
We're **deeply concerned** that Dad is still driving after his last two accidents.
The zoo said it was **deeply concerned** by the incident and had opened an investigation.

drill.sentence: Wildlife experts are {{deeply concerned}} about the sharp decline in monarch butterflies.
drill.hint: very worried (the adverb is not *very* or *seriously*)

entries.related: *gravely concerned* — even more formal and serious; *worried sick* — informal, extremely worried; *concerned for* + person — worried about their safety.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: The most important thing, which should be dealt with before anything else.
entries.usage: Common at work, in business and public life, and in personal planning: *Safety is our top priority.* Patterns are *be a top priority*, *make something a top priority* and *a top priority for* + person. With a possessive there is no article: *my top priority*.
entries.pattern: be (a / someone's) top priority; make something a top priority
examples: Finding a good pediatrician was **a top priority** when we moved to Denver.
The bakery's new owners say keeping the original recipes is their **top priority**.
When you travel with small kids, getting enough sleep becomes **a top priority**.

drill.sentence: After a string of bad reviews, the gym's new manager has made cleanliness {{a top priority}}.
drill.hint: the most important thing to deal with first (the adjective is not *high*)

entries.related: *a high priority* — important, but not necessarily the most; *first and foremost* — above all; *make something a priority* — decide to treat it as important.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To have to deal with a difficult situation or problem.
entries.usage: Common in news, business, sports and personal stories. The subject is the person or group in difficulty, and adjectives such as *serious, huge, new* or *unique* often go before *challenge*. Other patterns are *face the challenge of* + *-ing* and *face challenges* in the plural.
entries.pattern: face a (serious / huge / new) challenge; face the challenge of + -ing
examples: Small farms **face a huge challenge** when the price of fuel goes up.
As a single dad, he **faced the challenge** of working full time and raising three kids.
The new coffee shop **faces a tough challenge**: there are four others on the same block.

drill.sentence: Like many rural towns, ours {{faces the challenge}} of keeping young people from moving away.
drill.hint: has to deal with the difficulty (the noun is not *problem* or *task*)

mistake.wrong: Our team stands before a big challenge.
mistake.right: Our team faces a big challenge.
mistake.why: *Stand before a challenge* is a word-for-word translation of German *vor einer Herausforderung stehen*; English uses the verb *face*.

entries.related: *rise to the challenge* — deal with it successfully; *tackle* — start dealing with a problem actively; *pose a challenge* — be the cause of the difficulty.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: Able to be lost, damaged or won, depending on how a situation turns out.
entries.usage: Common in news, sports, business and serious conversation. Typical patterns are *X is at stake*, *there's a lot at stake* and *what's at stake*; the subject is what depends on the outcome, such as money, jobs, a title or a reputation. *At risk* focuses on danger and is common with people (*children at risk*).
entries.pattern: X is at stake; there's a lot / too much at stake; what's at stake
examples: With hundreds of jobs **at stake**, the whole town is following the talks to save the old paper mill.
Read the contract carefully; there's a lot of money **at stake**.
The family's farm was **at stake**, so they hired the best lawyer they could afford.

drill.sentence: Before the final, the coach reminded the players what was {{at stake}}: a trip to the national championship.
drill.hint: could be won or lost (two words; not *on the line*)

entries.related: *on the line* — informal, same idea; *at risk* — in danger of harm or loss; *high stakes* — with a lot to win or lose.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To express an idea or argument clearly in a discussion.
entries.usage: Very common in meetings, debates and conversation: *She made a good point.* Adjectives often go before *point* (*good, valid, interesting, fair*), and *make the point that* + clause states the idea. Don't confuse it with *make a point of* + *-ing*, which means to do something deliberately.
entries.pattern: make a (good / fair) point; make the point that + clause
examples: My son **made a good point**: why buy a second car if we both work from home?
In her talk, the nutritionist **made the point** that no single food will make you healthy.
During the town hall, a retired teacher **made an interesting point** about the cost of the new parking garage.

drill.sentence: At the PTA meeting, she {{made the point}} that the school spends far more on sports than on its library.
drill.hint: clearly stated the argument (the verb is not *raised*)

entries.related: *have a point* — be partly right; *get your point across* — make people understand you; *make a point of* + *-ing* — do something on purpose.

entries.label: adverb + adjective
entries.meaning: Strongly praised and advised by other people as very good or worth doing.
entries.usage: Common in reviews, travel guides, references and casual advice, and often used alone in reviews: *Highly recommended!* The active form is *I highly recommend it*, and a trusted person or business *comes highly recommended*. *Strongly recommended* sounds more like official advice: *Reservations are strongly recommended.*
entries.pattern: be highly recommended (by + someone); come highly recommended
examples: Our dentist was **highly recommended** by three different neighbors, so we gave her a try.
**Highly recommended!** The guide was funny, and the views from the trail were amazing.
The book is **highly recommended** for anyone starting their first job as a manager.

drill.sentence: This little taco place gets great reviews, and it was {{highly recommended}} by our hotel's front desk.
drill.hint: praised and suggested as very good (the adverb is not *strongly*)

entries.related: *strongly recommended* — similar, often for official advice; *come highly recommended* — be praised by people you trust; *a must-see* — informal, something you shouldn't miss.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To watch, listen to or think about something very carefully.
entries.usage: Common in instructions, teaching, health advice and news. The pattern is *pay close attention to* + noun or a *what / how* clause; *pay attention* is the basic form, and *close* makes it stronger. The verb is normally *pay*, and the preposition is always *to*.
entries.pattern: pay close attention to + noun / what … / how …
examples: **Pay close attention to** the road signs; the exit comes up fast after the bridge.
Investors are **paying close attention to** what the Federal Reserve says about interest rates.
If you **pay close attention to** how your baby cries, you'll learn to tell hunger from tiredness.

drill.sentence: When the flight attendant explains the safety rules, {{pay close attention to}} where the nearest exit is.
drill.hint: watch and listen very carefully to (verb + adjective + noun + preposition)

mistake.wrong: Please pay close attention on the details.
mistake.right: Please pay close attention to the details.
mistake.why: *Attention* takes *to*; learners often use *on* because of *focus on* or their first language.

entries.related: *keep an eye on* — informal, watch over time; *focus on* — direct all your attention to; *take note of* — notice and remember.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A sensible, relevant argument that deserves to be taken seriously, even if you don't fully agree.
entries.usage: Common in meetings, debates and polite disagreement: *That's a valid point, but …*. Typical patterns are *make / raise a valid point* and *You have a valid point*. It sounds a bit more formal and neutral than *a good point* or *a fair point*.
entries.pattern: make / raise / have a valid point
examples: That's **a valid point**, but we've already paid for the tickets.
One student raised **a valid point** about the lack of healthy food in the cafeteria.
The critics have **a valid point**: the movie is at least thirty minutes too long.

drill.sentence: Your brother has {{a valid point}}; if we leave at six, we'll miss the worst traffic.
drill.hint: a sensible argument (adjective + noun; the adjective is not *good* or *fair*)

entries.related: *a fair point* — conversational, admits the other side is partly right; *a good point* — the most common, casual; *beside the point* — not relevant.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: Physically present, face to face, rather than by phone, email or online.
entries.usage: Very common in speech and writing, especially since video calls became normal: *meet in person*, *apply in person*, *see someone in person*. Before a noun it is hyphenated: *an in-person meeting*. Don't confuse it with *personally*, which usually means "speaking for myself" or "directly involved".
entries.pattern: meet / apply / see someone in person; an in-person + noun
examples: We've talked on the phone for months, but we've never met **in person**.
In the US, you have to apply **in person** for your first passport, but you can usually renew by mail.
The singer looked much shorter **in person** than on TV.

drill.sentence: The first interview is on Zoom, but the final round is {{in person}} at the company's office in Austin.
drill.hint: with everyone physically there (not *on site* or *face-to-face*)

entries.related: *face to face* — similar, stresses direct contact; *in the flesh* — informal, often surprised; *virtually* — online, the opposite.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To find it hard to do something.
entries.usage: Neutral to slightly formal, and common in medical, school and official contexts: *Do you have difficulty breathing?* The next verb is an *-ing* form, sometimes after *in* (*have difficulty in sleeping*), though American English usually drops the *in*. With a noun, use *with*: *have difficulty with stairs*.
entries.pattern: have (some / great / no) difficulty + -ing; have difficulty with + noun
examples: Some international students **have difficulty finding** an apartment without a credit history.
Many new drivers **have difficulty parallel parking** on busy streets.
Tell your doctor if you **have any difficulty swallowing** after the procedure.

drill.sentence: After the stroke, my uncle {{had difficulty}} finding the right words, so we were patient with him.
drill.hint: found it hard (a formal noun; not *trouble*, *problems* or *a hard time*)

mistake.wrong: I have difficulty to concentrate in the afternoon.
mistake.right: I have difficulty concentrating in the afternoon.
mistake.why: After *have difficulty*, use the *-ing* form, not *to* + verb.

entries.related: *have trouble* + *-ing* — more casual, same grammar; *have a hard time* + *-ing* — informal, very common in American speech; *struggle to* + verb — stresses effort.

entries.label: adverb + adjective
entries.meaning: Knowing something completely and clearly, including what it means or what may result from it.
entries.usage: Common in formal speech, official writing and serious conversation, often to show that a risk or fact was known: *She was fully aware of the risks.* Patterns are *fully aware of* + noun and *fully aware that* + clause. Compared with *well aware*, it stresses complete knowledge, not that the fact is already familiar.
entries.pattern: be fully aware of + noun / that + clause
examples: Patients must be **fully aware** of the risks before they agree to the surgery.
We bought the old house **fully aware** that the roof would need replacing soon.
The company was **fully aware** of the defect but kept selling the car for two more years.

drill.sentence: When he took out the loan, he was {{fully aware}} of the high interest rate; nobody tricked him.
drill.hint: knowing all about it (the adverb is not *well* or *perfectly*)

entries.related: *well aware* — already knows, often said defensively: *I'm well aware*; *conscious of* — noticing or thinking about something; *in the dark* — informal, not aware.

entries.term: have a hard time doing something
entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To struggle to do something; to find it difficult.
entries.usage: Very common in American speech and informal writing, and more casual than *have difficulty*. The next verb is an *-ing* form: *I had a hard time finding parking.* Without *-ing*, *have a hard time* means to go through a difficult period, and *give someone a hard time* means to criticize or tease them.
entries.pattern: have a hard time + -ing; have a hard time with + noun
examples: I **had a hard time** falling asleep after that horror movie.
Small businesses are **having a hard time** finding workers who can start right away.
My dad **has a hard time** believing that people pay six dollars for a cup of coffee.

drill.sentence: The new kid in class is shy and is {{having a hard time}} making friends.
drill.hint: struggling (informal; not *trouble* or *difficulty*)

entries.related: *have difficulty* + *-ing* — more formal; *struggle to* + verb — stresses effort; *give someone a hard time* — tease or criticize them.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: Ordinary people in a society, as opposed to experts, officials or people with special access.
entries.usage: Common in news, official announcements, business and science communication. American English uses a singular verb (*The general public is …*), while British English often uses a plural one. Typical phrases are *open to the general public* and *members of the general public*.
entries.pattern: open / available to the general public; members of the general public
examples: The garden is private, but it's open to **the general public** on the first Sunday of every month.
The report is full of technical terms, so it's hard for **the general public** to understand.
The new phone will be available to **the general public** in March, after a test period with selected users.

drill.sentence: The country club's golf course is closed to {{the general public}} except during the annual charity tournament.
drill.hint: ordinary people who aren't members (three words with *the*)

entries.related: *the public* — same, shorter; *laypeople* — non-experts, a bit formal; *the average person* — one typical member of the public.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: At the latest possible moment, just before it is too late.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation and news, usually about plans that change, are canceled or are done late: *She canceled at the last minute.* Before a noun it becomes *last-minute* with a hyphen: *a last-minute change*. It often carries a slight criticism of poor planning.
entries.pattern: do / cancel / change something at the last minute; a last-minute + noun
examples: Our babysitter canceled **at the last minute**, so we had to skip the concert.
He always packs **at the last minute** and forgets something important.
The deal was saved **at the last minute** when both sides agreed to a shorter contract.

drill.sentence: I booked the flight {{at the last minute}}, so I paid almost twice the usual price.
drill.hint: just before it was too late (a prepositional phrase; not *at the eleventh hour*)

mistake.wrong: We changed our plans in the last minute.
mistake.right: We changed our plans at the last minute.
mistake.why: German *in letzter Minute* leads to *in*, but the fixed phrase uses *at*; *in the last minute* means during the final sixty seconds, for example of a game.

entries.related: *in the nick of time* — informal, just in time; *at the eleventh hour* — at the last moment, more dramatic; *ahead of time* — the opposite.

entries.term: have no choice but to do something
entries.label: verb phrase
entries.meaning: To be forced to do one particular thing because there is no other option.
entries.usage: Common in speech, news and official statements, often to justify an unpopular decision: *We had no choice but to cancel.* It is followed by *to* + verb. *Have no option but to* is a close, slightly more formal variant.
entries.pattern: have no choice but to + verb
examples: When the snowstorm closed the highway, we **had no choice but to** spend the night in a motel.
With rents rising every year, many young teachers **have no choice but to** live far from the schools where they work.
The referee **had no choice but to** stop the game when the lights went out.

drill.sentence: The restaurant lost its lease, and the owners {{had no choice but to}} close after thirty years.
drill.hint: could only do this one thing (the noun is not *option* or *alternative*)

entries.related: *have no option but to* — same, slightly more formal; *be forced to* — stresses outside pressure; *be left with no choice* — similar, common in news.

entries.label: noun phrase
entries.meaning: The worst possible thing that could happen in a situation.
entries.usage: Common in planning, business, medicine and conversation. Typical patterns are *the worst-case scenario is that* + clause, *in the worst-case scenario* and *prepare for the worst-case scenario*. In speech, *Worst case, …* is a casual short form, and *the best-case scenario* is the opposite.
entries.pattern: the worst-case scenario is that …; in the worst-case scenario; worst case, …
examples: **The worst-case scenario** is that we miss our connection and spend the night in Chicago.
Engineers designed the dam to survive **the worst-case scenario**: a major earthquake during a flood.
Before the surgery, the doctor walked us through **the worst-case scenario**, which helped us feel prepared.

drill.sentence: Don't panic about the job interview; {{the worst-case scenario}} is that you don't get it and keep looking.
drill.hint: the most terrible outcome you can imagine (hyphenated adjective + noun)

entries.related: *the best-case scenario* — the opposite; *if worse comes to worst* — if the worst thing happens; *a nightmare scenario* — a very bad possible outcome, dramatic.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To learn skills and knowledge over time by doing something in practice.
entries.usage: Common in job ads, career advice, résumés and interviews. Patterns are *gain experience in / with* + noun and *gain experience as* + role, often with *valuable, hands-on* or *practical*. *Get experience* is the casual equivalent.
entries.pattern: gain (hands-on / valuable) experience in / with + noun; gain experience as + role
examples: She volunteered at an animal shelter to **gain experience** before applying to vet school.
The internship is unpaid, but you'll **gain** a lot of hands-on **experience** with real clients.
Many chefs **gain experience** in several kitchens before they open their own restaurant.

drill.sentence: He took a part-time job at a bank to {{gain experience}} in customer service while finishing college.
drill.hint: learn practical skills by doing the work (the verb is not *get*)

mistake.wrong: I made a lot of experiences during my internship.
mistake.right: I gained a lot of experience during my internship.
mistake.why: German *Erfahrungen machen* leads to *make*; in this sense *experience* is uncountable and goes with *gain* or *get*.

entries.related: *get experience* — casual; *build skills* — develop abilities over time; *learn the ropes* — informal, learn the basics of a job.

entries.label: adverb + adjective
entries.meaning: Knowing something very well, usually already, so that it does not need to be pointed out.
entries.usage: Very common in speech and writing, often as *I'm well aware (of that)*, which can sound defensive or slightly irritated, as if to say "you don't need to tell me." It takes *of* + noun or a *that* clause. Compared with *fully aware*, it stresses that the knowledge is already familiar.
entries.pattern: be well aware of + noun / that + clause
examples: "Your shoelace is untied." "I'm **well aware**; I'm just trying not to drop three coffees."
Most smokers are **well aware** of the health risks, but quitting is still incredibly hard.
The restaurant owner is **well aware** of the parking problem, but there isn't much she can do about it.

drill.sentence: I'm {{well aware}} that the car is old, but it gets me to work and I don't have a monthly payment.
drill.hint: already know (the adverb is not *fully* or *perfectly*)

entries.related: *fully aware* — knows everything, often in formal contexts; *only too aware* — painfully aware of a problem; *conscious of* — noticing something.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To present information formally to a group of people, often with slides.
entries.usage: Common at work, at school and at conferences. The usual verb is *give*; *do a presentation* is casual, and *make a presentation* is also common, especially in business. The patterns are *give a presentation on / about* + topic and *to* + audience.
entries.pattern: give a presentation on / about + topic (to + audience)
examples: I have to **give a presentation** to the board on Monday, and I haven't finished my slides.
Each student will **give a short presentation** about a country they'd like to visit.
The park ranger **gave a presentation** on bears and how to store food safely at camp.

drill.sentence: My daughter is nervous because she has to {{give a presentation}} in front of the whole class tomorrow.
drill.hint: present a topic formally (the verb is not *do* or *make*)

mistake.wrong: Tomorrow I'll hold a presentation about our sales numbers.
mistake.right: Tomorrow I'll give a presentation about our sales numbers.
mistake.why: German *eine Präsentation halten* leads to *hold*; English uses *give* (or casually *do*), and *hold* goes with *a meeting* or *an event*.

entries.related: *deliver a presentation* — more formal; *present* — the one-word verb; *give a talk* — a speech to an audience, often less formal.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: Increasing in number, amount or level.
entries.usage: Common in news, reports and conversation about trends: *Rents are on the rise.* It usually follows *be*, and the subject is often something unwelcome, like prices, crime or cases of an illness, though not always. *On the increase* is a less common variant.
entries.pattern: X is / has been on the rise
examples: Bike thefts are **on the rise** in our neighborhood, so lock yours up even for five minutes.
Interest in cooking at home has been **on the rise** since the pandemic.
Concert ticket prices have been **on the rise** for years, and fans are fed up.

drill.sentence: Home prices in the area are {{on the rise}} again, so we may have to look farther from the city.
drill.hint: increasing (a prepositional phrase; not *on the increase* or *going up*)

entries.related: *on the increase* — same, less common; *on the decline* — decreasing; *rising* / *growing* — plain verb forms.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To have polite, light conversation about unimportant topics, such as the weather or weekend plans.
entries.usage: Very common in American social and work life: at parties, in elevators, with neighbors and before meetings. The verb is *make*, with no article: *make small talk with* someone *about* something. Many people say they hate small talk, but in the US it is an expected way to be friendly with strangers.
entries.pattern: make small talk (with + someone) (about + topic)
examples: While we waited for the elevator, my new neighbor **made small talk** about the heat wave.
I'm terrible at **making small talk** at weddings when I don't know anyone.
Before the interview started, the manager **made small talk** about the traffic.

drill.sentence: At the dinner party, I had to {{make small talk}} with a man who only wanted to discuss his golf game.
drill.hint: have light, polite conversation (verb + adjective + noun)

mistake.wrong: We made a small talk about the weather.
mistake.right: We made small talk about the weather.
mistake.why: *Small talk* is uncountable, so it takes no *a*.

entries.related: *chitchat* — informal, light talk; *break the ice* — start a conversation with a stranger; *catch up* — talk with a friend about recent news.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A general understanding or estimate that is not exact or detailed.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation and at work when asking for or giving an estimate: *Can you give me a rough idea of the cost?* Patterns are *have / give someone a rough idea of* + noun or a *wh-* clause. *A rough estimate* is used for numbers, and *a vague idea* suggests even less knowledge.
entries.pattern: give someone / have a rough idea of + noun / how much / when …
examples: Check the menu online before you go to get **a rough idea** of the prices.
I have **a rough idea** of the plot, but I've never actually read the book.
The tour guide gave us **a rough idea** of the city's history before we started walking.

drill.sentence: I don't need an exact time; just give me {{a rough idea}} of when you'll be home.
drill.hint: an approximate sense (the adjective is not *general*)

entries.related: *a ballpark figure* — informal, a rough number; *a vague idea* — even less exact; *a rough estimate* — an approximate number.

entries.label: adverb + adjective
entries.meaning: Used by many people or in many places.
entries.usage: Common in news, technical writing and product descriptions. It works after *be* (*This drug is widely used*) and before a noun (*a widely used app*). Other frequent pairs with *widely* are *widely known*, *widely accepted* and *widely available*.
entries.pattern: be widely used (in / by / for + noun); a widely used + noun
examples: This blood pressure medication is safe, cheap and **widely used**.
Baking soda is **widely used** for cleaning as well as for cooking.
"OK" is so **widely used** that people understand it in almost every country.

drill.sentence: WhatsApp is {{widely used}} in Europe and Latin America but less popular in the US.
drill.hint: relied on by huge numbers of people (adverb + participle; not *commonly*)

entries.related: *commonly used* — similar, slightly plainer; *widespread* — existing in many places, often for problems; *widely available* — easy to find or buy.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To slowly make people believe that they can rely on you, through consistent actions over time.
entries.usage: Common in talk about relationships, business, management, health care and public life. Patterns are *build trust with* + someone and *build trust between* + groups. It stresses time and effort; the opposite processes are *lose*, *break* or *erode trust*.
entries.pattern: build trust with / between + people
examples: Our accountant spent years **building trust** with her clients, and now most of them send their friends to her.
The new police chief walks the neighborhood every week to **build trust** with residents.
A good babysitter **builds trust** with the kids before the parents ever leave the house.

drill.sentence: Teachers who listen to their students and keep their promises {{build trust}} quickly.
drill.hint: make others feel they can rely on them (the verb is not *earn* or *gain*)

entries.related: *earn someone's trust* — get it through your own behavior; *gain trust* — similar; *break someone's trust* — the opposite, by betraying it.
